summary: Defines a management database module for monitoring mail services, extending the basic Network Services Monitoring MIB. It replaces RFC 1566 and was replaced by RFC 2789.

plainLanguage.summary: It adds mail-specific gauges to a general health chart, so managers can check on a mail server.

questions: what is the mail monitoring mib
how to monitor a mail server with snmp
what metrics does the mail monitoring mib track
subtitle: A standardized way to monitor mail servers using SNMP.

tldr.problem: Mail server operators need a standard way to monitor the health and activity of Message Transfer Agents (MTAs), including message counts, volumes, and error rates.
tldr.mechanism: The Mail Monitoring MIB extends the SNMP network management framework with tables that track MTA-specific metrics like received and transmitted messages, stored message volumes, and detailed errors.
tldr.outcome: Network administrators can use standard SNMP tools to monitor mail server operation. RFC 2789 superseded this with an updated version.

today: RFC 2249 is a Proposed Standard. It was superseded by RFC 2789, which provided further updates to the Mail Monitoring MIB.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2249 defines an extension to the SNMPv2 management framework specifically for monitoring Message Transfer Agents (MTAs)—the systems that route and deliver email. It extends the basic Network Services Monitoring MIB to track MTA performance and health.

The MIB allows operators to monitor MTAs at multiple levels: across the entire MTA or broken down into logical groups. Each group can represent a different communication channel, protocol, or destination, letting administrators see traffic flowing to different parts of their network.
sections.plainLanguage: This document adds mail server gauges to a general monitoring toolkit. It tells you which numbers to read on a mail server and what they mean.

sections.title: Message Flow and MTA Objects
sections.content:
MTAs process messages in a four-step flow. First, messages are received from various sources: user agents, message stores, other MTAs, or gateways. Second, the MTA determines the next hop—the destination to send the message toward (which may require duplication for multiple recipients). Third, the message may be converted into a format appropriate for the next hop. Fourth, the message is transmitted to its destination.

The MIB must account for the fact that different MTAs store messages at different points in this flow. Some expand messages as they arrive, while others store first and expand during retransmission. This means message counts at different stages do not always match.

The RFC defines four tables. The first two are mandatory: the mtaTable for overall MTA metrics and the mtaGroupTable for per-group metrics. The last two are optional: the mtaGroupAssociationTable (to track active connections) and the mtaGroupErrorTable (to count specific types of errors).
sections.plainLanguage: Mail servers handle messages in steps: receive, route, maybe convert format, then send. This RFC tracks how many messages and how much data flows through each step, at both the whole server level and at smaller groups within the server.

sections.title: The MIB Tables
sections.content:
The mtaTable tracks counters across the entire MTA: messages received, stored, and transmitted; the total volume (in kilobytes) of each; the number of recipients; the count of successful and failed format conversions; and the number of detected message loops (where a message will never be delivered and cycles endlessly).

The mtaGroupTable replicates these counters for each group, and adds more granular information: timestamps for the oldest message in the queue and the last time the group had inbound or outbound activity; counts of active and accumulated associations (network connections); rejection and failure reasons; the scheduled retry time; and the name and description of the group's peer or function.

Error tracking uses Enhanced Mail System Status Codes (from RFC 1893), which encode errors as three-part codes (class.subject.detail). This allows the mtaGroupErrorTable to count specific error types—such as authentication failures or syntax errors—separately for inbound, internal, and outbound traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB has a main score sheet for the whole mail server (how many messages came in, how many left, how many are stuck). It also lets you break that down into sections, with extra details like when the oldest waiting message arrived and how many times the server tried to connect somewhere.

sections.title: Conformance Levels
sections.content:
The RFC defines four conformance levels for SNMP implementations. The basic level implements the main mtaTable and mtaGroupTable. The association level adds tracking of active network connections. The error level adds detailed error counts. The full level implements all three.

This allows implementations to choose what level of monitoring detail they provide, from a basic count of messages to a complete audit trail of where errors occur.
sections.plainLanguage: You can implement this MIB at four levels: just the main numbers, main plus connections, main plus errors, or everything.

sections.title: Updates from RFC 1566
sections.content: RFC 2249 obsoletes RFC 1566 (the original Mail Monitoring MIB from 1994) with the following enhancements: clearer descriptions of fields; new fields for group description and URL; a distinction between the time of the last outbound connection attempt and the last successful connection; counters for message format conversions; an explicit hierarchy mechanism so groups can form tree structures; a full error tracking table with Enhanced Status Codes; the oldest message's ID in each queue; and per-MTA and per-group message loop counters.
sections.plainLanguage: The original version from 1994 was updated with more details about what's happening, where groups fit in the structure, and what kinds of errors occurred.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The MIB defines read-only access, so it cannot be used to change MTA behavior or attack a system. However, the information it exposes is passive but potentially revealing: it discloses the existence of mail services on a host, their type and configuration, and patterns of network usage. An attacker could use this data to detect vulnerabilities or analyze traffic patterns.

Access to the MIB should be restricted to authorized administrators only.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB can only read data, not change anything, so it is safe from direct attacks. But someone who sees the numbers could guess what kind of mail server it is and how busy it is.
